claims.text: The starting nanoalloy is equiatomic Co–Cr–Fe–Ni–Cu.
High-temperature homogenization produces an initially homogeneous Co–Cr–Fe–Ni–Cu nanoalloy.
Rapid quenching after annealing preserves a uniform elemental distribution.
A uniform elemental distribution corresponds to a single-phase structure in this nanoalloy.
Rapid quenching kinetically freezes atomic positions.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion by limiting atomic mobility.
Suppressed diffusion prevents elemental segregation during cooling.
Slow cooling over several hours permits greater atomic mobility than rapid quenching.
The atomic mobility available during slow cooling enables individual elements to diffuse.
Diffusion during slow cooling leads to elemental segregation.
Segregation during slow cooling can initiate secondary-phase formation.
Relative to slowly cooled samples, rapidly quenched samples will have greater elemental homogeneity and less segregation.
Relative to rapidly quenched samples, slowly cooled samples will exhibit larger compositional fluctuations and incipient phase separation.
Residual stresses or cooling-related experimental artifacts may alter apparent elemental uniformity independently of diffusion kinetics.

contradictions.description: The intervention and conditions specify water quenching for the rapid-cooling group, whereas the boundary states that cooling occurs within an inert atmosphere. Water quenching is not cooling within an inert atmosphere.
